The following is a transcript from Steve Wieck's post on the Prince's
Conclave mailing list addressing why the North American championship
was to be changed to a two-day. PLEASE NOTE: this message was sent
on OCTOBER 14 of 2004 and represented preliminary thinking, which may
differ from the decisions eventually arrived at. I copy it because
it is the best source of summary information about the thinking that
went into the change.

You will note that the focus is basically on what the best format for
determining a continental champion was and no consideration is being
placed on how this will affect badge fees for the competitor. In
general, I would say that playing for a continental championship
involves playing a lot of games at fancy venues so I don't really
agree with your problem. The years I've gone to Gencon, I've seen a
lot of people running around the place who don't seem to consider
themselves independently wealthy, but it does cost something, yes.
Maybe not everyone can afford that but then, not everyone has to play
for the big championship, either. Considering what you're doing, I
don't see the beef.

> From: "Steve Wieck" <ste...@white-wolf.com>
> To: "'Conclave'" <conc...@list.white-wolf.com>
> Subject: VEKN Conclave - Draft of New Championship and Australian
> Qualifier Rules for Princes to Review
> Date: Thu, 14 Oct 2004 15:52:36 -0700
>
> Princes,
>

> Two policy changes that need your input and suggestions for any changes
> before they are made into a final version.
>

> Steve Wieck
> WW
>
>

> ------------------------------------------
> Large Championship Tournaments Process
>

> Why Change?
> -------------------
> In very large tournaments such as the EC and NAC many players believe
> that 3 rounds of play is too few to properly select finalists and a
> Champion.
>

> Also, many believe that it very large tournaments, you must play a
> high-risk, high-yield deck type to reach the finals, which limits the
> deck variety that is brought to play to decks that can not just get
> table wins but also get table sweeps.
>

> It is believed that the Championship selection process would be improved
> by adding more rounds to the large tournaments.
>

> A group of past and present EC and NAC organizers have discussed many
> proposed solutions and what follows is the end result of those
> discussions.
>
> The proposal is offered to the Conclave at large to discuss and make
> suggestions for the next two weeks. Feedback form the Princes will then
> be incorporated into a final policy which will be effective in 2005 and
> forward, but WILL NOT CHANGE EC 2004!
> WILL NOT CHANGE EC 2004!
> WILL NOT CHANGE EC 2004!
> WILL NOT CHANGE EC 2004!
>

> What is the Proposed Policy?
> ---------------------------------------
> Continental Qualifiers are unchanged. For Continental Championship
> events there will be 2 formats for 2005.
>

> 1. The Traditional Format will continue to be used for the Australian
> and South American Championships. There are no changes for these events.
>

> 2. The North American Championship (which will be held again at Gen Con
> Indy) and the European Championship (In Budapest) will become 3 days of
> events instead of 2.
>

> For the NAC, the Last Chance Qualifier (LCQ) will move to Thursday.
> The Championship Round 1 will be Friday. This will be a
> standard 3+F event. It will earn the standard Continental Championship
> rating coefficient for player ratings purposes.
> The top 40 players from Round 1 will advance to Round 2 of the
> Championship on
> Saturday.
> For Round 2, players may change their decks and all standings, VPs,
> etc,. from Round 1 are ignored. Round 2 is played as a standard 3+F and
> its finals determine the 2005 North American Champion.
>

> For the EC, this will be the same except the event will probably run
> from Friday to Sunday. If the EC 2005 organizers face difficulties in
> making the event 3 days, then we will submit a contingency plan for
> Prince review if that happens.
>
>
>

> Australian Qualifiers
>

> The proposal is offered to the Conclave at large to discuss and make
> suggestions for the next two weeks. Feedback form the Princes will then
> be incorporated into a final policy which will be effective in 2005 and
> forward.
>

> Why Change?
> -------------------
> Australian players feel that their VTES community was better served by
> the prior Qualifier rules (top 50% on nonquals, max 10) than the new one
> (top 25% of nonquals).
>

> What is the Proposed Policy?
> -----------------------------------------
> 1. Australian Continental Qualifiers go back to using the prior rule for
> the number of players who qualifiy for the AC from all regional
> Australian Continental Qualifiers
> 2. Players at Australian Qualifiers must still have placed in the top
> 25% of nonquals in order to be considered qualified for any other
> Continental Championship event (any such event other than Australia's).
>
>

> We will begin organizing 2005 Qualifiers after November 1st. Please do
> not ask about 2005 Qualifiers at this time.
>

> Regards,
>
> Steve

I do not know if all of these bullets were ultimately resolved as Steve
laid out, here. Some may have gotten altered during or after the conclave
discussion of them.

Fred

Messages.Author: Rehlow
Messages.Body:


Vampire being popular and not a dead game is at fault. It is now a 2
day championship because of the number of participants. I think I can
best explain with an example (these numbers are probably not entirely
accurate for North America, but maybe).

Lets pretend it is a 1 day championship and 100 people show up. In
order to make the top five you will (most likely) need 3 TW and
probably 12-15 VPs. How likely is it that combat decks can pull that
off? Wall decks? Decks that aren't stealth bleed? Pretty boring
championship if you "have" to play stealth bleed to have any shot at
the final table.

Now lets look at the 2 day championship. Again 100 people show up for
day 1, but this time 40 people (last I heard it was 40) qualify for day
2. You can now play any tourny worthy deck and have a reasonable chance
of making the top 40. Now day 2 is only 40 players large and you don't
need 3 sweeps to make the finals of the NA championship. More deck
diversity = better championship at least IMHO.

Now if only 41 people show up for day 1, the 2 day championship will be
pretty lame, but lets hope not. And maybe I'm wrong and only 20 people
from day 1 will qualify, I'm pretty sure we'll have a good deal more
than 20 for day 1.

As an aside, if you want to spend $60 (badge) + $18 (3x $6 event
tickets) on a box of cards instead, why don't you just come to GenCon
and volunteer to demo Vampire at the White Wolf booth when you're not
playing in tournaments. I heard they gave a box of boosters to those
that ran the demos at Origins (I don't know what the time commitment
was to get a box though).

Later,
~Rehlow

Yes, I see what you're getting at. If reducing the cost for participants
is a priority, you're right: a better way to do that would be to hold the
NAC at some other venue. In theory, they could even hold it alongside
Gencon at another venue in Indianapolis over the same days. That way,
people who want to go back and forth could still do that.

I don't know exactly what considerations lead White Wolf to do the NAC
the way they do. However, were I the one in charge, I would be want
the maximum exposure for my game which translates into having my big
year-end super-cool championship-of-da-hol'-woild tournament actually
take place _in_ the biggest game convention of the year where lots of
players, retailers, and game business luminaries could see it on the
schedule and in the flesh. I think it's especially impressive that
scores of players are sitting around playing in a single tournament
and if that tournament is a 2-day affair, so much the better. That may
not be much help for you in the short run, but if it drums up more
business in the long run, that means more players for us and hence,
more opportunities to play. Anyway, just my $0.02. I don't really
know one way or the other, myself.

Fred

Exactly. :) Hey, if the Olympics can rotate, then so can the NAC. :)

We spent about 8 years running tournaments at our local convention.
Eventually the numbers started to dwindle. We started paying $40+ to
pay the admission into a place where we'd play 4 V:TES tournament and
then go home. The problem was that we were playing with the same people
that showed-up to our home playgroup. We hung on for a couple of extra
years thinking it was worth the entrance fee because we were
"advertising". We eventually came to the conclusion that we gained few
new players at the convention and that could be made-up for in other
ways.

We went through the same thing again trying to support GenCon So. Cal.
We spent a ton of money to go to that crappy con and play V:TES. The
only way we could even get the right tables was to go in the far corner
of some kiddie area. NO-ONE saw V:TES played at GenCon So. Cal and we
players footed the bill for the sake of advertisement.

Now we run our events outside of the convention. We have some devoted
players who *work at* advertising and creating newbies instead of
crossing our fingers and hoping that the convention does the hard work
for us. Now we have a $15 admission instead of $40+. Now we use the
admission for tons of prizes instead of leasing the convention's
tables.

V:TES is an unusual character. I don't think it operates like other
CCGs. Whether that's because of the complexity or the game length, the
average age or income of the players, I dunno. I think we'd do just
fine without "advertising" by holding the NAC at GenCon.

A few points regarding the possibility of moving the NAC from GenCon:

- First off I just want to point out that a lot of the "me too"
responses regarding a rotating system come from European players, who
almost certainly are not representative of most North American VTES
players. I don't expect the European Championship to base their
location and scheduling based solely on my personal convenience and I
don't imagine that catering to international convenience is at the list
of priorities for the South American and Australian Championships.

- Secondly, while a rotating system certainly does have several
advantages, the process of selecting a location can be extremely
cumbersome. This can quickly boil down to lame politicking where
political alliances (and not the merits of each location) seem to take
the forefront. As examples of this, I point to discussions concerning
the Great Lakes Qualifier this past year and the European Championships
from a few years ago.

communication concerning discussion of the most recent Great Lakes

observer, I was also frustrated by all those "hey, vote for me this

conventions. From my experiences at Origins and GenCon, I consistantly
see people watching the game who turn out to have played years ago and
didn't realize that the game was still alive. In fact, this past month

So...just playing Devil's Advocate as always.

Actually, I do not feel like *I* was shafted at all. I don't mind
traveling for VTES so it wouldn't have made a big difference to me

Illinois, Michigan, or Wisconsin. I was attending two Qualifiers before
the Great Lakes Qualifier (New Jersey and Boston) and I qualified at
the Boston Qualifier so by the time the GL Qualifier had rolled around,
it's not as if I had a personal stake in qualifying.

I do feel like *someone* got shafted though (which is one of the main
reasons I'm continuing to push the issue). This year, I think it was
really Wisconsin and Minnesota players that totally got the shaft. In
2005 we have had or will have Qualifiers in Lafayette, IN, Columbus,
OH, and Indianapolis, IN. If you live in the Indiana/Ohio area it's
great to have 3 qualifiers all within a few hours worth a drive. If
you're in Wisconsin or Minnesota for example, you're pretty much shit
out of luck.

In regards to the GL Qualifier discussion, I initiated a group e-mail
on September 6th, 2004. Initially we had a good response, with 17
e-mails up till September 10th. Then there was absolutely no response
until September 22nd. It was also around this time that we decided to
get non-Prince feedback by posting on the newsgroup. By early November
we still had not reached consensus and Milwaukee dropped out of the
race to get the discussion going. By late November we still hadn't
gotten very far and getting people to talk about the issue felt like
pulling teeth. Even by the end of December things still had not been
finalized (regarding where to hold the event). In the end, we needed to
get the U.S. National Coordinator involved who finally helped put the
issue to rest at the end of January. Maybe I'm just completely out of
my mind but it's my personal opinion that it should *not* take 5 months
to choose a location and finalize it. By the end of January I was still
regularly getting e-mails and calls from players in Ohio, Boston,
Atlanta, and Colorado asking me "what the hell is up with the Great
Lakes Qualifier?"

Of course there were some excellent "face-to-face chats between more
than 2 of the Princes." Then again when one Indiana Prince jokingly
referred to those chats as "sooper-secret discussions", we ended up
with a Michigan Prince getting "riled up" about the issue. And then we
had the one Illinois Prince who was definitely way too pushy about the
issue and trying to rush his proposal through because his convention
staff were "forcing" him to make a hurried decision.

participating in VTES *after* the Qualifier discussion was finished up.

that he felt he really needed the Qualifier in order to maintain
interest in his playgroup. He didn't get the Qualifier, his playgroup
is defunct, and he resigned as Prince. I'm sure you can connect the
dots.

As I plainly said on the newsgroup then and reiterate now, my initial
preference was towards Chicago. But after Ankur and Jill stressed the
importance of "fairness" (during one of those much lauded "face-to-face
chats") I came to the realization that the "fairest" choice would be

I suppose you need to know the story of qualifiers in the Northeast.

The first Northeast Regional Qualifier (in 2001) was held in East
Rutherford, NJ by Stephen Buonocore. Stephen had to step away from the
game, so a vacancy for the qualifier opened up. Both I (then the
Prince of Boston) and Grant Garvin (the Prince of Seekonk, MA, also
serving the Providence, RI area) had separate proposals to host a New
England Regional, but when Stephen bowed out, it meant that whatever
qualifier we ran would serve the entire Northeast, so we decided to
work together on it starting in 2002. Grant did the coordination with
TotalCon (as he'd done a lot of work with them in the past, and
suggested that con in the first place) and I headed up the judging. We
worked together again in 2003, and in both years, I was annoyed that
people called it "the Boston qualifier", since I felt it did a
disservice to the work Grant, from the separate Seekonk/Providence
playgroup, had put into it. In 2004, Grant took a break from the game,
and I ran the qualifier with the help of Ben Spaulding, the Prince of
Bangor, Maine (he was already qualified, having been a finalist at the
2003 NAC, and offered to help judge). In 2005, I was no longer Prince
of Boston, having accepted the role of US National Coordinator, and so
Josh Feuerstein, the third Prince of Boston, ran the Northeast Regional
Qualifier at TotalCon.

In the years of running the qualfier at TotalCon, there weren't any
alternate proposals from other playgroups to run the qualifier, as far
as I remember. However, Nick Watkins of NYC expressed interest in
having an additional qualifier that would serve the NY/NJ/PA
"tri-state" area, as in his opinion there was a large enough and
separate enough base of players to support it. He contacted me, Josh
Duffin, and Chad Brown (and possibly others) about the idea, and it was
eventually decided to have David Lapp of New Jersey host a 2004
qualifier in New Jersey, in addition to the qualifiers in Massachusetts
and DC. It was a big success, so he ran another one in 2005, which had
unfortunately low attendance due to a major snowstorm that shut down
the Northeast. I very much hope he or someone else runs a qualifier in
that area next year, as it's abundantly clear that there are enough
people in that area to support it.

Speaking of which, I would also be in favor of re-doing the regions in
that area to have a New England Region (CT, RI, MA, VT, NH, ME) and a
Tri-State Region (PA/NY/NJ). If WW doesn't like that, I'm all in favor
of continuing to have the additional NJ qualifier, much as there's an
additional qualifier at Origins. As much as MA, NJ, and DC are fairly
close together, the fact of the matter is that the base of players in
those areas are large enough and separate enough to support their
qualifiers on their own.

So, the Northeast Regional Qualifiers at TotalCon have not at all
been an exclusively Boston thing, but rather they've been a
collaborative effort in New England. In addition, we were (and will
continue to be) very supportive of the creation of the new qualifier in
the region. As US National Coordinator, I'm very open to the idea of
re-organizing states to better suit their needs with respect to
regional qualifiers. So, if Ohio or any other state is looking to
change their region, please contact me.

- Ben Peal, US National Coordinator

Messages.Author: Ankur Gupta
Messages.Body:
I'm not sure why I'm responding to this really. The issues are done and
we're hijacking the Gencon thread. I do think however that you have blown
this thing far out of proportion. I didn't feel as much politicking as
you're suggesting, and I certainly don't think that the last word on the
issue ought to be what I just read. There were lots of discussions,
compromises, and generally good teamwork that went into the GLQ; that
needs to be highlighted, not overshadowed by these kinds of negative
comments. Infighting, politicking, and shennanigans weren't hallmarks of
the GLQ process, and I won't brook any suggestion to that effect.

I'd also just like to point out that the GLQ is consistently a really
large event. For the past 3 years running, we've had an attendance of 40+
players, hailing from across the region. From my impressions, that seems
like the third-largest qualifier in the states (with GenCon and Origins
being the largest ones). We also have a region with *four* very active,
very large playgroups. We may take longer to settle on a location, but
we're democratic and we put forth a fantastic event each year with stellar
attendance. As you can see from other responses, there just isn't as much
vtes or as many strong playgroups who *want* to host elsewhere in the
country.

This fact is a positive statement for the Great Lakes. That it comes along
with a certain amount of additional overhead (choosing the location) is to
be expected. We take pride in our qualifier, and we want to make sure we
put our best foot forward each year. Sometimes it takes organizational
time to decide which that is, as we collectively understand what we can
offer to the region.

> I do feel like *someone* got shafted though (which is one of the main
> reasons I'm continuing to push the issue). This year, I think it was
> really Wisconsin and Minnesota players that totally got the shaft. In
> 2005 we have had or will have Qualifiers in Lafayette, IN, Columbus, OH,
> and Indianapolis, IN. If you live in the Indiana/Ohio area it's great to
> have 3 qualifiers all within a few hours worth a drive. If you're in
> Wisconsin or Minnesota for example, you're pretty much shit out of luck.

By this logic then, if the qualifier is not in Wisconsin or Minnesota each
year, they will be shafted each year. GenCon and Origins will not change
locations in the forseeable future. Are you then suggesting that it be in
either WI or MN each year? If we're going to make a generic decision based
upon recurring events such as the ones you've mentioned, then there is in
fact no decision to be made:

Each year should be set in the northern part of the GL region, and
definitely no further south than Milwaukee.

And, as far as I know, we discussed the option of a fixed qualifier
location, and from my understanding, the GL has decided to rotate. This
decision was made years ago, but certainly well before discussions were
begun about 2005. Does this preclude Chicago's bid? Possibly, but note
that as a region, we didn't exclude that choice. Cause we're nice people
like that.

Anyway, a rotating qualifier system has the consequence that sometimes
some people have to drive longer distances, and other years, shorter
distances. It happens. This year WI and MN players got "the shaft". Next
year, it will likely be someone else. Only teleportation can save us from
this. I'm working on it, but until then, the vtes community will just have
to drive.

> my mind but it's my personal opinion that it should *not* take 5 months
> to choose a location and finalize it. By the end of January I was still
> regularly getting e-mails and calls from players in Ohio, Boston,
> Atlanta, and Colorado asking me "what the hell is up with the Great
> Lakes Qualifier?"

The above paints an unnecessarily over-dramatic picture. There were no
disasters, so no need to have this happen.

> Of course there were some excellent "face-to-face chats between more
> than 2 of the Princes." Then again when one Indiana Prince jokingly
> referred to those chats as "sooper-secret discussions", we ended up with
> a Michigan Prince getting "riled up" about the issue. And then we had

First off, I don't appreciate the mocking way in which you consider the
face-to-face discussions. Perhaps you weren't privy to them, but certainly
they were serious, on-topic, and addressed issues. Many princes, and all
of the ones who wanted to host (with the exception of David) were there.
We had a good talk, and opened things up.

Perhaps I should have recognized that David might have felt left out of
the loop (since he wasn't there), and not have joked about said
conversation in the newsgroup post you reference, but this was a
*five-minute* misunderstanding, over what you describe as an arduous
affair taking 5 months or so. Are you really trying to suggest that this
had anything to do with anything? I don't think David took any real
slight, and it was clear after a moment that no such was actually
intended. (As proof of that, David graciously brought me Thai food at the
qualifier while I was judging and didn't poison it. I still owe him for
that. . . .)

> You mentioned "a very specific proposal" from Lafayette. I actually
> remember quite the opposite. For *quite some time* I was suggesting that
> each of the potential venues do some research and actually provide some
> potential plans instead of simply saying "hey we'll do a qualifier." For
> a long time there were few takers willing to actually supply details.

The very specific proposal was in fact, quite specific. So were proposals
from other domains, either via the newsgroup, personal e-mail, or
face-to-face discussions. Each indicated some estimate on costs,
availability, weekends in question, accomodations, driving considerations,
beer, and women. I think it was quite sufficient to make a decision. I'm
certainly not going to put in effort 6 months in advance of a qualifier to
schedule rooms, track down hotels and get price quotes, reserve a venue
location, find a topless bar willing to run a special vtes edge program,
and hit up players for other information if we're not running a qualifier.

It's silly to suggest that princes go to these lengths. The proposals were
as specific as was necessary during the planning phase. I can't imagine
what more you might want. Perhaps you are of the opinion that the
qualifier should have been fully organized by the end of 2004. Regardless
of the timeframe, your organizational constraints are your opinion and
should be interpreted as such, rather than as some implied failure of the
GL region to organize an event in some reasonable time frame.

> In a discussion with that Prince several months afterward, he told me
> that he felt he really needed the Qualifier in order to maintain
> interest in his playgroup. He didn't get the Qualifier, his playgroup is
> defunct, and he resigned as Prince. I'm sure you can connect the dots.

I feel bad for Rob Sachs because recruiting is hard, but we (as a region)
can't decide to hold the qualifier in location X because doing otherwise
would kill the local playgroup in X. If he needed tournaments to maintain
interest, he should have run tournaments. Which, to my knowledge, was not
done more than once during his entire tenure as a prince. Recruiting and
maintaining a playgroup involves more than just lobbying for a qualifier;
qualifiers have a different purpose. He should have traveled or encouraged
traveling to the *VERY* nearby Chicago domain for the non-trivial number
of tournaments which were held there, or north to the tournaments in MI
that are only 1-1.5 hours away. If they really needed tournament exposure,
they could have come to the newbie rich Lafayette in 2 hours and played
here. I never once saw anyone from that troupe at any of those
tournaments. Between the three domains (two of which were extremely
close), there have been lots of tournaments at regular intervals. If rides
were an issue, carpooling was probably an option. Trains were available
from Chicago to Lafayette for $12. . . . There are lots of options and
always have been.

There are no dots to connect here except the ones which you're attempting
to force upon this community through some perceived associative guilt. A
qualifier's purpose is not to maintain interest of a fledgeling domain.
That's a prince's job.

> As I plainly said on the newsgroup then and reiterate now, my initial
> preference was towards Chicago. But after Ankur and Jill stressed the
> importance of "fairness" (during one of those much lauded "face-to-face
> chats") I came to the realization that the "fairest" choice would be
> Milwaukee (though by that point they were no longer interested in
> hosting).

Fairness insomuch as the region had *already* decided to rotate. (See
previous years.) Suddenly stopping, therefore, would be perceived as
unfair. I'm glad you decided that Milwaukee would be the fairest choice.
Note that that decision suggests that you had already prioritized the
myriad concerns in running a qualifier. Your priority list may not match
others. So, it came down to the fact that you had a vote in the ultimate
choice. You exercised your vote and affected the process. That's what
people do. (Whether that was an appropriate vote is another matter that
I'll discuss in a minute.)

> There was a slipshod and unscientific vote tally on the newsgroup which
> ended up which a valid vote tally of : 3 Chicago, 2 Milwaukee, 5

Slipshod and unscientific? Prove it. There's no need for an accusation of
this sort, especially when great care was taken to handle the voting and
reporting. If you had issue with the process, you should have brought it
to me privately, rather than over this public forum. I can assure you that
no mistakes were made (and corrections were solicited in the case that
some were made). I'm not sure how one becomes more scientific than say,
counting votes of people, making sure that they aren't spoofing, checking
every possible place a vote may have been cast, and enumerating the tally
once it was done. With some small understanding of the scientific method
as a Ph.D. candidate, I can't fathom any more care could have been taken.
Even then, if there were mistakes made, there was a clear place for
them to be corrected. No one indicated any disagreement with the tally.

If you took issue with the fact that only princes could vote, you need to
recognize how untenable it is for players in a region to uniformly vote on
such an issue. If you require votes according to states, you'll note that
each major playgroup of the Great Lakes Region is in a different state. If
you fall back to the most reasonable voting scheme, you then weight each
prince's votes based upon their playgroup's size. In such a measure, there
were certain votes which shouldn't have been admissable/worth much. If I
might add, yours was among the ones which was tenuous based upon that
metric. Just food for thought.

> Lafayette. One other Prince and myself voted for Milwaukee out of
> principle (even though it had withdrawn from the race), though Chicago
> was both of our second choices. And even then I pointed out that we had
> not even come to a consensus on *how* a vote should be conducted. (Based
> on # of Princes? # of players? # of states?).

Votes for Milwaukee were irrelevant, because at the time votes were
solicited, it was explicitly stated that Milwaukee was not a choice. Jill
had already graciously pulled Milwaukee's bid. Who's politicking then by
further obscuring the decision-making process to rehash decided issues?
We're trying to decide a qualifier here, not implement some method for
civil disobedience.

As far as deciding how the voting should take place, I think that once we
put forth at the table that we want to maximize GLQ attendance, we leave
it to each prince to consider their own capability to decide the best
choice consistent with those constraints. We are working together as a
team, and everything doesn't have to be spelled out if the intentions are
good. This is a fair assumption to make, since we're only trying to create
the best damned event the Great Lakes can manage.

> So all of this is why I'm more than a little jaded about the painfully
> frustrating process of selecting a venue. If one region had such a tough
> time, one can only imagine how arduous selecting a championship venue
> would be.

I think that the process was far less painful than you think. If you're
posting on behalf of someone who was well and truly of the opinion that
they were shafted, let them post. Your reasonings don't convince me that
this was the case. Maybe theirs will, and we can make appropriate
adjustments for next year.

> P.S. I also want to state, for the record, that I was unfortunately not
> able to attend this year's Great Lakes Qualifier because of a
> last-minute obligation that came up. My absence had nothing to do with

Eric, I certainly didn't conclude any perceived slight based upon your
attendance at the GLQ. Not everyone thinks this way, and it's insulting to
presume that others do/did. Most people probably didn't even care.
Moreover, I'm not sure why its relevant to the discussion.

> had attended that Qualifier the past two years before). Sadly enough
> however, there are some players in the Great Lakes region who *will*
> refuse to attend tournaments out of spite or due to perceived slights.
> These players will also complain incessently about how some playgroups
> "never" attend their events when that is totally untrue.

Why is this a needed component of your argument? These kinds of vague
accusations can really be hurtful, as someone might ask themselves, "Is he
talking about me?", even when it's not directed at that person. The
newsgroup is not a place to air dirty laundry in unrelated threads. Your
post should not contain jabs and slights. It should not contain hints to
other issues which aren't even relevant to the topic at hand. You should
not present biased, unfair comments detailing one side of the irrelevant
issue in an unrelated thread.

I don't fully know what's going on with this comment, but you have almost
certainly angered some people with it. I would apologize if I were you.

Bottom line, Eric: Do you really feel that the GL region isn't working
together? I don't feel that. We all run tournaments. We all travel. We all
play vtes. If you have issues with individual people, take it to those
people. Don't make a bad name for the GL region because things didn't
progress the way you wanted. Or perhaps make some constructive suggestions
to improve the process.

I personally am glad to be around great people. The GL is full of helpful,
friendly folks who are happy to oust you at a moment's notice. There are
many veterans, solid players, and enthusiastic new entrants to vtes. We
have a supportive region. Personally speaking, all of the neighboring
domains have been very encouraging as Lafayette grew. That comraderie is
not only present, it is growing. We have a regular GL-only trophy in the
Sandwich Tournament Series, and there are tournaments within a hundred
miles of any playgroup on a regular basis. I don't know that any other
region can claim such things.

For the record, the Great Lakes region is a hard-working region. We foster
vtes at all levels, have good communication, and generally work and play
well together. I think we did a fine job this year in qualifier-related
issues. I think we did a fine job last year as well. I think we did a fine
job the year before that. We're all about doing fine jobs.

We plan to continue to do what we do best. And as such, I don't want
anyone to think that we are anything else other than what we are. . . a
solid, strong region with a cohesive organizational structure. After all,
there's no way we could have such a consistantly well-attended qualifier
otherwise.

Ankur Gupta

I'm not saying take VtES out of Gencon, I'm merely stating that
something as player specific as a National Championship (and a Week of
Nightmares as well), that caters to the majority of an experienced
player base, should be conceived from a mindset that benefits said
group. I personally don't feel that Gencon is that answer. I've also
recently have gotten heavily into German board gaming and the appeal of
going to Gencon to only play VtES is becoming less and less appealing.
That said, even if nothing changed, I would still continue to go to
Gencon (WoN) and continue only playing VtES because that time spent
with all the other players in priceless to me and I enjoy the
camaraderie of hanging with all the other great players almost as much
as I enjoy VtES it's self. So I'm just saying to have that experience
while visiting other parts of North America, or even going only to
Atlanta if WW chooses to do it close to home for $ reasons, while not
feeling like my whole Gencon experience is gone because I choose to
hang with the VtES crowd, would be more beneficial to the overall
VtES/Gamers experience. Keep VtES at Gencon. Keep the presence of
tournaments there. Focus on getting new players; I'll volunteer my time
to help. But the National Championship combined with the WoN should be,
I believe, a separate less expensive event altogether.

Again, just my $.02
***JediMike***

less important than the overall incentive to even attend the event.

Yes, it would require more planning to make a WoN rotate along with the
NAC. The WoN could probably be done for less $$$ and the accomodations
could be perfectly suited, etc. For example, back in Milwaukee we had
the best WoN at a perfectly designed hotel that was 20 minutes away
from GenCon. With a rotating NAC, the host city would choose a location
for the NAC that also had a perfectly designed hotel that is close by,
inexpensive, geek friendly, or whatever. All factors could be taken

back to wondering which V:TES players are going to GenCon for something
other than V:TES. Or more precisely, I'd like to see the future a few
years down the road and see what a rotating NAC and WoN would look like
as well as how GenCon would fare.

I certainly can't say with any certainty what the outcome would be if
the plan were adopted. But I can tell you that I'd personally be
happier if the event rotated. I'll enjoy having it closer to home once
in a while and I'll enjoy visiting other V:TES communities when it
isn't close to home.
Maybe I'm just getting older but my favorite part of GenCon is hanging
out with players away from the con itself. I won't miss the excitement
and spectacle of the BigCon (tm) and would prefer a NAC location that
felt more like the big WoN from a few years back.

I'm not sure where to throw this in... here seems as good a place as any.

As some of you already know, I live in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, which is
frankly not a big V:tES hotspot. In fact, with a few occasional exceptions,
I am pretty much the only player, and travel to play more often than I get
to play here.

It is, however, a perfect place to host a convention-style tournament. The
downtown economy is somewhat geared to support our casino, which frankly
isn't doing as well as the city had hoped. As a result, we have plenty of
relatively cheap hotel rooms, places to host events, and lots of restaurants
and nightclubs etc. It is the perfect place to host smallish conventions, or
an event such as the NAC.

Windsor is centrally located, relative to many major cities. We're right
across the river from Detroit, four hours eastish of Chicago, four hours
westish of Toronto. There are shuttles to and from Detroit Metro Airport.

Because Canada is a third world country *cough*, the exchange rate is
favourable for US visitors. In fact, most local businesses deal in both $CDN
and $USD. I can't say for sure, speaking as a resident, but I would think
that a few days stay here would be a lot cheaper on the whole than
Indianapolis, GenCon or no.

So, if there is to be consideration of moving the NAC around the continent a
bit, I'll put this out there. I would be very happy to help organize the
event here, if there is sufficient interest. I'm assuming the powers-that-be
that make such decisions will notice this post and hang on to it for future
reference.

Cheers,

It might be reasonable, or a good suggestion to make to a host city, but
I don't think that stipulating it as a hard-and-fast requirement is
necessarily a good idea.

As a worst-case example, imagine that one year you have two cities
saying they want to run the NAC.

One city has a fairly lack-lustre approach, which effectively has a
hotel they can book, a couple of crates of boosters for some draft
events and not a lot else. But it does meet the criteria of having a
WoN plan - get up and play V:TES every day, go to bed.

The other city can't manage a whole week off - the main organisers in
that city simply couldn't get the time from work. But they could put
together a four day weekend which was jam-packed with stuff - a rolling
set of 2R+F tournaments starting every couple of hours, a Build-Your-
Own-Storyline tournament that they've spent time and effort creating
beautiful "proxy" cards for to represent key factors in the storyline
tied in with their location, a hotel happy about doing a couple of
social events (a barbecue round the pool or whatever), a decent bulk
discount to make the hotel more affordable, organised a local singles
seller/trader who's happy to come along with his stock one afternoon in
